claim: The inward-rectifier Kir2.1 channel in brain capillary endothelial cells (cECs) plays a major role in neurovascular coupling (NVC) by mediating a neuronal activity-dependent, propagating vasodilatory (hyperpolarizing) signal.
source: We recently reported that the inward-rectifier Kir2.1 channel in brain capillary endothelial cells (cECs) plays a major role in neurovascular coupling (NVC) by mediating a neuronal activity-dependent, propagating vasodilatory (hyperpolarizing) signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and represents a previously established finding.

claim: Kir2.1 activity is suppressed by depletion of plasma membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: We further demonstrated that Kir2.1 activity is suppressed by depletion of plasma membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Ca2+/Na+-permeable TRPV4 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 4) channels are expressed in cECs.
source: Here, we report that Ca2+/Na+-permeable TRPV4 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 4) channels are expressed in cECs and are tonically inhibited by PIP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including patch-clamp recordings and knockout mouse experiments.

claim: TRPV4 channels in cECs are tonically inhibited by PIP2.
source: Here, we report that Ca2+/Na+-permeable TRPV4 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 4) channels are expressed in cECs and are tonically inhibited by PIP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that PIP2 analogs inhibit TRPV4 currents and that PIP2 depletion activates TRPV4 channels.

claim: Depletion of PIP2 by agonists that promote PIP2 hydrolysis through Gq-protein-coupled receptors (GqPCRs) causes simultaneous disinhibition of TRPV4 channels and suppression of Kir2.1 channels.
source: We further demonstrate that depletion of PIP2 by agonists, including putative NVC mediators, that promote PIP2 hydrolysis by signaling through Gq-protein-coupled receptors (GqPCRs) caused simultaneous disinhibition of TRPV4 channels and suppression of Kir2.1 channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing simultaneous monitoring of TRPV4 and Kir2.1 currents in response to GqPCR agonists.

claim: GqPCR activation functions as a molecular switch to favor capillary TRPV4 activity over Kir2.1 signaling.
source: These findings collectively support the concept that GqPCR activation functions as a molecular switch to favor capillary TRPV4 activity over Kir2.1 signaling, an observation with potentially profound significance for the control of cerebral blood flow.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing opposite effects of PIP2 depletion on TRPV4 and Kir2.1 channels.

claim: Intermediate and small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels (IK and SK, respectively) are important in transducing elevations in intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) into membrane potential hyperpolarization in artery/arteriolar ECs.
source: Notably, intermediate and small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels (IK and SK, respectively), which are important in transducing elevations in intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) into membrane potential hyperpolarization in artery/arteriolar ECs to cause relaxation of electrically coupled smooth muscle cells (Ledoux et al., 2008; Sonkusare et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2003), are absent in brain cECs (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IK and SK channels are absent in brain cECs.
source: Notably, intermediate and small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels (IK and SK, respectively), which are important in transducing elevations in intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) into membrane potential hyperpolarization in artery/arteriolar ECs to cause relaxation of electrically coupled smooth muscle cells (Ledoux et al., 2008; Sonkusare et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2003), are absent in brain cECs (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Signaling through G protein–coupled receptors of the Gαq/11-subtype (GqPCRs) is robust in brain cECs.
source: However, signaling through G protein–coupled receptors of the Gαq/11-subtype (GqPCRs)—an important component of this smooth muscle regulatory axis—is robust in brain cECs (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: In the canonical pathway of GqPCR signaling, Gαq released upon agonist binding activates phospholipase C (PLC), which hydrolyzes PIP2.
source: In the canonical pathway of GqPCR signaling, Gαq released upon agonist binding activates phospholipase C (PLC), which hydrolyzes the minor inner leaflet phospholipid, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about GqPCR signaling pathways.

claim: Breakdown of PIP2 yields diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3).
source: Breakdown of PIP2 yields diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), the latter of which increases [Ca2+]i by acting on its cognate receptor (IP3R) on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to promote Ca2+ release from intracellular stores.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about PIP2 hydrolysis.

claim: IP3 increases [Ca2+]i by acting on its cognate receptor (IP3R) on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to promote Ca2+ release from intracellular stores.
source: Breakdown of PIP2 yields diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), the latter of which increases [Ca2+]i by acting on its cognate receptor (IP3R) on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to promote Ca2+ release from intracellular stores.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about IP3 signaling.

claim: Brain capillaries act as a neuronal activity-sensing network.
source: We recently reported that brain capillaries act as a neuronal activity-sensing network, demonstrating that brain cECs are capable of initiating an electrical (hyperpolarizing) signal in response to neuronal activity that rapidly propagates upstream to dilate feeding parenchymal arterioles and increase blood flow locally at the site of signal initiation (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Brain cECs are capable of initiating an electrical (hyperpolarizing) signal in response to neuronal activity that rapidly propagates upstream to dilate feeding parenchymal arterioles.
source: We recently reported that brain capillaries act as a neuronal activity-sensing network, demonstrating that brain cECs are capable of initiating an electrical (hyperpolarizing) signal in response to neuronal activity that rapidly propagates upstream to dilate feeding parenchymal arterioles and increase blood flow locally at the site of signal initiation (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Extracellular K+ is the critical mediator of capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling.
source: We also established the molecular mechanism underlying this process, showing that extracellular K+—a byproduct of every neuronal action potential—is the critical mediator and identifying the Kir2.1 channel as the key molecular player (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The Kir2.1 channel is the key molecular player in capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling.
source: We also established the molecular mechanism underlying this process, showing that extracellular K+—a byproduct of every neuronal action potential—is the critical mediator and identifying the Kir2.1 channel as the key molecular player (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Kir2.1 channels are activated by external K+ and exhibit steep activation by hyperpolarization.
source: Kir2.1 channels are activated by external K+ and exhibit steep activation by hyperpolarization (Hibino et al., 2010; Longden and Nelson, 2015), characteristics that facilitate regenerative K+ conductance in neighboring cECs and enable long-range propagation of the hyperpolarizing signal (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreases in capillary endothelial PIP2 levels induced by GqPCRs agonists suppress Kir2.1 channel currents.
source: Intriguingly, we have since discovered that decreases in capillary endothelial PIP2 levels induced by GqPCRs agonists suppress Kir2.1 channel currents, reflecting the fact that PIP2 is required for Kir2.1 channel activity (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: PIP2 is required for Kir2.1 channel activity.
source: Intriguingly, we have since discovered that decreases in capillary endothelial PIP2 levels induced by GqPCRs agonists suppress Kir2.1 channel currents, reflecting the fact that PIP2 is required for Kir2.1 channel activity (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The suppressive effect of PIP2 depletion exerts a major modulatory influence on K+-evoked hyperemic responses in vivo.
source: Importantly, this suppressive effect of PIP2 depletion exerts a major modulatory influence on K+-evoked hyperemic responses in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors (implied from context).

claim: PIP2 binding has been shown to inhibit several members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of non-selective cation channels, including TRPV4.
source: Notable in this context, PIP2 binding has been shown to inhibit several members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of non-selective cation channels, including the vanilloid subtype TRPV4 (Nilius et al., 2008; Rohacs, 2009; Takahashi et al., 2014), which we and others have shown is an important Ca2+ influx pathway in arterial and arteriolar ECs (Earley and Brayden, 2015; Sonkusare et al., 2014;Sonkusare et al., 2012; White et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TRPV4 is an important Ca2+ influx pathway in arterial and arteriolar ECs.
source: Notable in this context, PIP2 binding has been shown to inhibit several members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of non-selective cation channels, including the vanilloid subtype TRPV4 (Nilius et al., 2008; Rohacs, 2009; Takahashi et al., 2014), which we and others have shown is an important Ca2+ influx pathway in arterial and arteriolar ECs (Earley and Brayden, 2015; Sonkusare et al., 2014;Sonkusare et al., 2012; White et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Kir2.1 channel appears to be the major K+ channel type in brain cECs.
source: The Kir2.1 channel appears to be the major K+ channel type in brain cECs (Longden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: TRPV4 channels in cECs exhibit an exceedingly low open probability under basal conditions due to tonic inhibition by PIP2.
source: Here, we show that TRPV4 channels are present in cECs and exhibit an exceedingly low open probability under basal conditions due to tonic inhibition by PIP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing single-channel recordings and the effects of PIP2 on TRPV4 activity.

claim: TRPV4 inhibition by PIP2 is relieved through PIP2 depletion, independent of the action of the PIP2 hydrolysis products, DAG and IP3.
source: We have further found that this inhibition is relieved through PIP2 depletion, independent of the action of the PIP2 hydrolysis products, DAG and IP3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using PKC inhibitors and Ca2+ chelators.

claim: PIP2 exerts opposite effects on TRPV4 and Kir2.1 channels in brain cECs.
source: Collectively, our findings indicate that PIP2 exerts opposite effects on TRPV4 and Kir2.1 channels in brain cECs, demonstrating that a single regulatory pathway governs the balance between two divergent signaling modalities—one depolarizing and the other hyperpolarizing—in the capillary endothelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing simultaneous monitoring of TRPV4 and Kir2.1 currents.

claim: GSK1016790A (GSK101) is a selective TRPV4 agonist.
source: We previously reported that the selective TRPV4 agonist GSK1016790A (hereafter GSK101) is a potent activator of TRPV4 currents in mesenteric artery ECs that induces maximal arterial dilation at concentrations in the low nanomolar range (Sonkusare et al., 2014; Sonkusare et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: GSK101 is a potent activator of TRPV4 currents in mesenteric artery ECs that induces maximal arterial dilation at concentrations in the low nanomolar range.
source: We previously reported that the selective TRPV4 agonist GSK1016790A (hereafter GSK101) is a potent activator of TRPV4 currents in mesenteric artery ECs that induces maximal arterial dilation at concentrations in the low nanomolar range (Sonkusare et al., 2014; Sonkusare et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: GSK101 at concentrations up to 100 nM failed to stimulate a detectable TRPV4 current in isolated cECs in the perforated whole-cell configuration.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that GSK101 was unable to evoke a detectable whole-cell TRPV4 current in cECs at concentrations that maximally activate TRPV4 channels in mesenteric artery ECs; in fact, even GSK101 concentrations as high as 100 nM failed to stimulate a detectable TRPV4 current in isolated cECs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Breaking through the cell membrane from a perforated patch in the presence of 100 nM GSK101 resulted in the gradual (~5 min) development of a robust TRPV4 current.
source: However, we serendipitously found that breaking through the cell membrane from a perforated patch in the presence of an otherwise ineffective GSK101 concentration (100 nM) resulted in the gradual (~5 min) development of a robust TRPV4 current, suggesting that a factor that suppresses TRPV4 channels had been washed out of the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: In the conventional whole-cell configuration with physiological levels of Mg-ATP (1 mM) included in the patch pipette, application of 100 nM GSK101 failed to evoke an outward current.
source: In the conventional whole-cell configuration with physiological levels of Mg-ATP (1 mM) included in the patch pipette, application of 100 nM GSK101 also failed to evoke an outward current.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 100 nM GSK101 caused the gradual (~4–5 min) development of a robust outward current in the conventional whole-cell configuration when Mg-ATP was omitted from the pipette solution.
source: In striking contrast, this same concentration of GSK101 caused the gradual (~4–5 min) development of a robust outward current in the conventional whole-cell configuration when Mg-ATP was omitted from the pipette solution (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Intracellular Mg-ATP (1 mM) caused a dramatic shift in the sensitivity of cEC TRPV4 channels to GSK101, with the EC50 of GSK101 for TRPV4 channels in the presence of Mg-ATP being 415 nM.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, intracellular Mg-ATP (1 mM) caused a dramatic shift in the sensitivity of cEC TRPV4 channels to GSK101: at a potential of 100 mV, the EC50 of GSK101 for TRPV4 channels in the presence of Mg-ATP was 415 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In the absence of Mg-ATP, the EC50 of GSK101 for TRPV4 channels was reduced ~23 fold to 18 nM.
source: However, in the absence of Mg-ATP, the EC50 was reduced ~23 fold to 18 nM (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), a value comparable to that observed in mesenteric artery ECs (Sonkusare et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The suppressive effect of ATP was specific for adenosine nucleotides, as inclusion of 1 mM GTP in the patch pipette did not alter currents.
source: The suppressive effect of ATP was specific for adenosine nucleotides, as inclusion of 1 mM GTP in the patch pipette did not alter currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GSK101-induced currents were completely abolished by the selective TRPV4 channel antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM).
source: GSK101-induced currents were completely abolished by the selective TRPV4 channel antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM) and were absent in cECs from TRPV4-knockout (TRPV4-/-) mice (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1), confirming that these currents are attributable to TRPV4 channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GSK101-induced currents were absent in cECs from TRPV4-knockout (TRPV4-/-) mice.
source: GSK101-induced currents were completely abolished by the selective TRPV4 channel antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM) and were absent in cECs from TRPV4-knockout (TRPV4-/-) mice (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1), confirming that these currents are attributable to TRPV4 channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The inhibitory effect of intracellular Mg-ATP (1 mM) suppressed both inward and outward currents in cECs activated by the TRPV4 agonist 4α-phorbol 12,13-didecanoate (4α-PDD; 5 µM).
source: The inhibitory effect of intracellular Mg-ATP (1 mM) was not limited to GSK101-activated TRPV4 currents. As shown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), it also suppressed both inward and outward currents in cECs activated by the TRPV4 agonist 4α-phorbol 12,13-didecanoate (4α-PDD; 5 µM, in the absence of RuR).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no detectable whole-cell TRPV4 current in the absence of a TRPV4 activator.
source: There was no detectable whole-cell TRPV4 current in the absence of a TRPV4 activator (Figure 1A), suggesting that these channels have a very low basal open probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TRPV4 channels in cECs have a very low basal open probability.
source: There was no detectable whole-cell TRPV4 current in the absence of a TRPV4 activator (Figure 1A), suggesting that these channels have a very low basal open probability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that no detectable current was observed without an activator.

claim: The unitary current amplitude of TRPV4 channels in cECs in the presence of GSK101 was 4.6 ± 0.3 pA (n = 3).
source: The unitary current amplitude in the presence of GSK101, estimated from amplitude histograms, was 4.6 ± 0.3 pA (n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The single-channel conductance of TRPV4 channels in cECs is 92 ± 6 pS.
source: This value corresponds to a single-channel conductance of 92 ± 6 pS, in line with values reported in an earlier investigation of TRPV4 channels in native arterial ECs (Watanabe et al., 2002) and heterologous expression systems (Loukin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: cECs held at +50 mV and dialyzed with Mg-ATP (1 mM) displayed infrequent openings (NPO = 0.038 ± 0.006).
source: cECs held at +50 mV and dialyzed with Mg-ATP (1 mM) displayed infrequent openings (NPO = 0.038 ± 0.006), but removing ATP increased single-channel opening by ~6 fold (NPO = 0.209 ± 0.044) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Removing ATP increased single-channel opening by ~6 fold (NPO = 0.209 ± 0.044).
source: cECs held at +50 mV and dialyzed with Mg-ATP (1 mM) displayed infrequent openings (NPO = 0.038 ± 0.006), but removing ATP increased single-channel opening by ~6 fold (NPO = 0.209 ± 0.044) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Single-channel openings in the absence of agonist exhibited a unitary current of 4.5 ± 0.3 pA at +50 mV.
source: Single-channel openings in the absence of agonist exhibited a unitary current of 4.5 ± 0.3 pA at +50 mV (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), similar to that evoked using a specific TRPV4 agonist (4.6 pA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and corresponding to a conductance of 90 ± 6 pS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Single-channel currents recorded in the absence of GSK101 were inhibited by the TRPV4 blocker HC-067047 (NPO = 0.063 ± 0.028).
source: Single-channel currents recorded in the absence of GSK101 were inhibited by the TRPV4 blocker HC-067047 (NPO = 0.063 ± 0.028) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 3), confirming their identity as TRPV4 channel-mediated currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Capillary TRPV4 channels have a basal open probability (PO) of ~0.0002.
source: Based on our estimate of ~225 functional TRPV4 channels per cEC (see Materials and methods), we calculate that capillary TRPV4 channels have a basal open probability (PO) of ~0.0002.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from experimental data.

claim: Replacing ATP in the patch pipette with the poorly hydrolyzable analog, ATP-γ-S (1 mM), resulted in GSK101 (100 nM) increasing TRPV4 currents to the same extent as observed in cells dialyzed with 0 mM Mg-ATP.
source: To test whether TRPV4 suppression requires ATP hydrolysis, we replaced ATP in the patch pipette with the poorly hydrolyzable analog, ATP-γ-S (1 mM). Under these conditions, GSK101 (100 nM) increased TRPV4 currents to same extent as observed in cells dialyzed with 0 mM Mg-ATP, indicating that ATP hydrolysis is required for channel inhibition (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required for TRPV4 channel inhibition.
source: To test whether TRPV4 suppression requires ATP hydrolysis, we replaced ATP in the patch pipette with the poorly hydrolyzable analog, ATP-γ-S (1 mM). Under these conditions, GSK101 (100 nM) increased TRPV4 currents to same extent as observed in cells dialyzed with 0 mM Mg-ATP, indicating that ATP hydrolysis is required for channel inhibition (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog does not inhibit TRPV4.

claim: Replacing Mg-ATP in the patch pipette with the Na+ salt of ATP (Na-ATP, 1 mM) while eliminating Mg2+ from the pipette solution abolished the suppressive effect of ATP.
source: Consistent with this prediction, replacing Mg-ATP in the patch pipette with the Na+ salt of ATP (Na-ATP, 1 mM) while eliminating Mg2+ from the pipette solution abolished the suppressive effect of ATP (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting the contribution of a kinase to this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor H-89 (1 µM) did not affect TRPV4 currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP.
source: On the basis of these observations, we next tested the involvement of protein kinases by bath-applying the protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor H-89 (1 µM), protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitor KT5823 (1 µM), or protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor calphostin C (0.5 µM). We then monitored outward TRPV4-mediated currents as described above. None of these inhibitors affected currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 2), ruling out a role for these protein kinases in TRPV4 inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitor KT5823 (1 µM) did not affect TRPV4 currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP.
source: On the basis of these observations, we next tested the involvement of protein kinases by bath-applying the protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor H-89 (1 µM), protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitor KT5823 (1 µM), or protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor calphostin C (0.5 µM). We then monitored outward TRPV4-mediated currents as described above. None of these inhibitors affected currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 2), ruling out a role for these protein kinases in TRPV4 inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor calphostin C (0.5 µM) did not affect TRPV4 currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP.
source: On the basis of these observations, we next tested the involvement of protein kinases by bath-applying the protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor H-89 (1 µM), protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitor KT5823 (1 µM), or protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor calphostin C (0.5 µM). We then monitored outward TRPV4-mediated currents as described above. None of these inhibitors affected currents in cells dialyzed with Mg-ATP (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 2), ruling out a role for these protein kinases in TRPV4 inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lower concentrations of Mg-ATP (10 and 100 µM) failed to effectively inhibit TRPV4 currents in cECs.
source: Further support for this conclusion is provided by the observation that lower concentrations of Mg-ATP (10 and 100 µM)—which activate the majority of protein kinases (Knight and Shokat, 2005)—failed to effectively inhibit TRPV4 currents in cECs (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The cellular levels of PIP2 are maintained through an ATP-hydrolysis–dependent process.
source: Thus, the cellular levels of PIP2 are maintained through an ATP-hydrolysis–dependent process (Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Hilgemann, 1997; Suh and Hille, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wortmannin (50 µM) significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP.
source: To assess the possible involvement of this pathway in capillary TRPV4 suppression, we tested the effects of four structurally unrelated pharmacological inhibitors of PI4K: wortmannin (50 µM), PIK93 (300 nM), phenylarsine oxide (PAO; 30 µM), and LY294002 (300 µM). In each case, inhibitors of PIP2 synthesis significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1), despite the high intracellular Mg-ATP concentration (1 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIK93 (300 nM) significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP.
source: To assess the possible involvement of this pathway in capillary TRPV4 suppression, we tested the effects of four structurally unrelated pharmacological inhibitors of PI4K: wortmannin (50 µM), PIK93 (300 nM), phenylarsine oxide (PAO; 30 µM), and LY294002 (300 µM). In each case, inhibitors of PIP2 synthesis significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1), despite the high intracellular Mg-ATP concentration (1 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Phenylarsine oxide (PAO; 30 µM) significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP.
source: To assess the possible involvement of this pathway in capillary TRPV4 suppression, we tested the effects of four structurally unrelated pharmacological inhibitors of PI4K: wortmannin (50 µM), PIK93 (300 nM), phenylarsine oxide (PAO; 30 µM), and LY294002 (300 µM). In each case, inhibitors of PIP2 synthesis significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1), despite the high intracellular Mg-ATP concentration (1 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LY294002 (300 µM) significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP.
source: To assess the possible involvement of this pathway in capillary TRPV4 suppression, we tested the effects of four structurally unrelated pharmacological inhibitors of PI4K: wortmannin (50 µM), PIK93 (300 nM), phenylarsine oxide (PAO; 30 µM), and LY294002 (300 µM). In each case, inhibitors of PIP2 synthesis significantly reversed TRPV4 channel inhibition by ATP (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1), despite the high intracellular Mg-ATP concentration (1 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At concentrations below those necessary to inhibit PI4K, wortmannin (0.1 µM) and LY294002 (10 µM) failed to increase TRPV4 current in cECs.
source: Notably, at concentrations below those necessary to inhibit PI4K (but sufficient to suppress phosphoinositide 3-kinases), the inhibitors wortmannin (0.1 µM) and LY294002 (10 µM) failed to increase TRPV4 current in cECs (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DiC8-PIP2 inhibited GSK101-induced TRPV4 currents, reducing them by 70–80% at concentrations of 10 to 50 µM.
source: To directly test whether PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels in cECs, we introduced the water-soluble, short acyl chain dioctanoyl PIP2 (diC8-PIP2) via the patch pipette. In the absence of Mg-ATP, diC8-PIP2 inhibited GSK101-induced TRPV4 currents, reducing them by 70–80% at concentrations of 10 to 50 µM (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The longer-chain PIP2 analog, diC16-PIP2 (10 µM), produced similar inhibition of TRPV4 currents as diC8-PIP2.
source: Similar inhibition was observed with the longer-chain PIP2 analog, diC16-PIP2 (10 µM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Scavenging endogenous, negatively charged PIP2 with intracellular poly-L-lysine (3 µg/ml) attenuated Mg-ATP effects on GSK101-induced TRPV4 currents.
source: Moreover, scavenging endogenous, negatively charged PIP2 with intracellular poly-L-lysine (3 µg/ml, molecular weight 15,000–30,000), included in the patch pipette, attenuated Mg-ATP effects on GSK101-induced TRPV4 currents (Figure 3E,F; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: PIP2 inhibits both GSK101-induced and constitutive TRPV4 channel activity in cECs.
source: Taken together, these data show that PIP2 inhibits both GSK101-induced and constitutive TRPV4 channel activity in cECs.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental data showing PIP2 effects on TRPV4.

claim: PGE2 significantly increased TRPV4 single-channel open probability in the absence of GSK101.
source: PGE2 significantly increased TRPV4 single-channel open probability in the absence of GSK101 (Figure 4A,B), increasing NPO ~6 fold (Figure 4C; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B,C.

claim: PGE2 increased TRPV4 NPO ~6 fold.
source: PGE2 significantly increased TRPV4 single-channel open probability in the absence of GSK101 (Figure 4A,B), increasing NPO ~6 fold (Figure 4C; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Application of PGE2 (2 µM) in the presence of GSK101 greatly increased TRPV4 currents in cECs dialyzed with Mg-ATP.
source: As predicted, application of PGE2 (2 µM) in the presence of GSK101 greatly increased TRPV4 currents in cECs dialyzed with Mg-ATP (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Currents evoked by PGE2 application were inhibited by the TRPV4 antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM).
source: Currents evoked by PGE2 application were inhibited by the TRPV4 antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM) and were absent in cECs from TRPV4-/- animals, confirming that they are mediated by TRPV4 channels (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Currents evoked by PGE2 application were absent in cECs from TRPV4-/- animals.
source: Currents evoked by PGE2 application were inhibited by the TRPV4 antagonist HC-067047 (1 µM) and were absent in cECs from TRPV4-/- animals, confirming that they are mediated by TRPV4 channels (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Introduction of the PIP2 analog diC8-PIP2 (10 µM) in the pipette solution prevented the increase in TRPV4 currents by PGE2.
source: Introduction of the PIP2 analog diC8-PIP2 (10 µM) in the pipette solution or inhibition of PLC using U73122 (10 µM)—pharmacological interventions that serve to compensate for or prevent PLC-dependent PIP2 degradation, respectively—prevented the increase in TRPV4 currents by PGE2 (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of PLC using U73122 (10 µM) prevented the increase in TRPV4 currents by PGE2.
source: Introduction of the PIP2 analog diC8-PIP2 (10 µM) in the pipette solution or inhibition of PLC using U73122 (10 µM)—pharmacological interventions that serve to compensate for or prevent PLC-dependent PIP2 degradation, respectively—prevented the increase in TRPV4 currents by PGE2 (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The non-selective prostanoid receptor (EP1/EP2/EP3) antagonist AH6809 (10 µM) prevented the effect of PGE2 on TRPV4 currents.
source: The non-selective prostanoid receptor (EP1/EP2/EP3) antagonist AH6809 (10 µM) also prevented this effect of PGE2, as did the selective EP1 antagonist SC51322 (1 µM), suggesting that PGE2 acts through the EP1 receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The selective EP1 antagonist SC51322 (1 µM) prevented the effect of PGE2 on TRPV4 currents.
source: The non-selective prostanoid receptor (EP1/EP2/EP3) antagonist AH6809 (10 µM) also prevented this effect of PGE2, as did the selective EP1 antagonist SC51322 (1 µM), suggesting that PGE2 acts through the EP1 receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PGE2 acts through the EP1 receptor to activate TRPV4 channels.
source: The non-selective prostanoid receptor (EP1/EP2/EP3) antagonist AH6809 (10 µM) also prevented this effect of PGE2, as did the selective EP1 antagonist SC51322 (1 µM), suggesting that PGE2 acts through the EP1 receptor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the effects of EP1 antagonists on PGE2-induced TRPV4 activation.

claim: U73343, the inactive analog of the PLC inhibitor U73122, did not alter PGE2 effects on TRPV4 currents.
source: U73343, the inactive analog of the PLC inhibitor U73122, did not alter PGE2 effects (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The PKC inhibitors, Gö6976 (1 µM) and calphostin C (0.5 µM), did not alter PGE2-induced activation of TRPV4 channels.
source: To rule out the involvement of these pathways in the PGE2-induced increase in TRPV4 currents, we first tested the effects of the PKC inhibitors, Gö6976 (1 µM) and calphostin C (0.5 µM), and found that neither altered PGE2-induced activation of TRPV4 channels (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Blocking Ca2+ reuptake into intracellular stores by inhibiting the SERCA pump with cyclopiazonic acid (CPA; 30 µM) did not attenuate PGE2-induced disinhibition of TRPV4 channel activity.
source: To determine whether intracellular Ca2+ signals downstream of EP1-PLC activation by PGE2 are involved in TRPV4 disinhibition, we blocked Ca2+ reuptake into intracellular stores by inhibiting the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) pump with cyclopiazonic acid (CPA; 30 µM) or by rapidly chelating cytoplasmic Ca2+ with BAPTA (5.4 mM). Neither maneuver attenuated PGE2-induced disinhibition of TRPV4 channel activity (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 2), arguing against a major contribution of DAG-PKC or IP3-Ca2+ signaling to this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rapidly chelating cytoplasmic Ca2+ with BAPTA (5.4 mM) did not attenuate PGE2-induced disinhibition of TRPV4 channel activity.
source: To determine whether intracellular Ca2+ signals downstream of EP1-PLC activation by PGE2 are involved in TRPV4 disinhibition, we blocked Ca2+ reuptake into intracellular stores by inhibiting the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) pump with cyclopiazonic acid (CPA; 30 µM) or by rapidly chelating cytoplasmic Ca2+ with BAPTA (5.4 mM). Neither maneuver attenuated PGE2-induced disinhibition of TRPV4 channel activity (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 2), arguing against a major contribution of DAG-PKC or IP3-Ca2+ signaling to this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PGE2 activates EP1 receptors and downstream PLC to deplete PIP2 and thereby relieve TRPV4 channel inhibition, independently of PIP2 metabolites.
source: Taken together, our data show that PGE2 activates EP1 receptors and downstream PLC to deplete PIP2 and thereby relieve TRPV4 channel inhibition, independently of PIP2 metabolites.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental data showing the pathway of PGE2 action.

claim: Carbachol (10 µM) induced an increase in TRPV4 currents comparable to that produced by PGE2.
source: Carbachol (10 µM), which can signal through Gq-coupled muscarinic receptors, induced an increase in TRPV4 currents comparable to that produced by PGE2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that GqPCR-mediated TRPV4 activation is not restricted to prostanoid EP1 receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The purinergic receptor agonist, ATP (50 µM), did not affect TRPV4 channel activity.
source: However, neither the purinergic receptor agonist, ATP (50 µM), nor the protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2)-activating peptide, SLIGRL-NH2 (5 µM), affected TRPV4 channel activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2)-activating peptide, SLIGRL-NH2 (5 µM), did not affect TRPV4 channel activity.
source: However, neither the purinergic receptor agonist, ATP (50 µM), nor the protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2)-activating peptide, SLIGRL-NH2 (5 µM), affected TRPV4 channel activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Application of PGE2 (2 µM) enhanced TRPV4 currents and simultaneously inhibited Kir2.1 currents.
source: In this setting, application of PGE2 (2 µM) enhanced TRPV4 currents and simultaneously inhibited Kir2.1 currents (Figure 6A,B; Figure 6—source data 1) compared with matching time controls, which showed no significant change in either current (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The onset of changes in TRPV4 and Kir2.1 currents in response to PGE2 was rapid (<60 s).
source: The onset of changes in TRPV4 and Kir2.1 currents in response to PGE2 was rapid (<60 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: TRPV4 activation and Kir2.1 suppression were kinetically comparable, with times for half-maximal change in activity (t0.5) of 3.4 min for TRPV4 and 4.4 min for Kir2.1 channels.
source: A kinetic analysis revealed that TRPV4 activation and Kir2.1 suppression were kinetically comparable, with times for half-maximal change in activity (t0.5) of 3.4 min for TRPV4 and 4.4 min for Kir2.1 channels, and corresponding time constants (τ) of 4.9 and 6.4 min, respectively (Figure 6C; Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The muscarinic receptor agonist carbachol (10 µM) facilitated TRPV4 currents and inhibited Kir2.1 currents.
source: The muscarinic receptor agonist carbachol (10 µM) similarly facilitated TRPV4 currents and inhibited Kir2.1 currents (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Purinergic receptor stimulation with ATP did not affect TRPV4 currents despite inhibiting Kir2.1 currents.
source: In contrast, purinergic receptor stimulation with ATP did not affect TRPV4 currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3) despite inhibiting Kir2.1 currents (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), as we reported previously (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The repertoire of functional ion channels in brain cECs remains incompletely characterized.
source: The repertoire of functional ion channels in brain cECs remains incompletely characterized, although certain molecular features have recently come into focus.
evidence: This claim represents a general statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: In arterial and arteriolar ECs, TRPV4 channel-mediated Ca2+ influx is closely linked to activation of Ca2+-sensitive SK and IK channels and subsequent membrane potential hyperpolarization.
source: In arterial and arteriolar ECs, TRPV4 channel-mediated Ca2+ influx is closely linked to activation of Ca2+-sensitive SK and IK channels and subsequent membrane potential hyperpolarization (Sonkusare et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Because cECs lack functional Ca2+-activated K+ channels, TRPV4-mediated influx of Na+/Ca2+ in these cells would lead to membrane potential depolarization.
source: However, because cECs lack functional Ca2+-activated K+ channels (Longden et al., 2017), TRPV4-mediated influx of Na+/Ca2+ in these cells instead would lead to membrane potential depolarization (Behringer et al., 2017; Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the absence of Ca2+-activated K+ channels in cECs and citations to previous studies.

claim: The TRPV4 channel is a major depolarizing element in cECs.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that the TRPV4 channel is a major depolarizing element in cECs, although we cannot rule out the possibility that other, as yet unidentified, cation channels may contribute to membrane depolarization, as suggested by earlier studies (Csanády and Adam-Vizi, 2004; Popp and Gögelein, 1992; Csanády and Adam-Vizi, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Lipid kinases involved in PIP2 synthesis require millimolar ATP for their activity.
source: It is well established that lipid kinases involved in PIP2 synthesis require millimolar ATP for their activity (Balla and Balla, 2006; Hilgemann, 1997; Knight and Shokat, 2005; Suer et al., 2001), and it has been amply demonstrated that PIP2 maintenance is dependent on ATP in multiple cell types (Suh and Hille, 2008; Ye et al., 2018; Zakharian et al., 2011), including cECs (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIP2 maintenance is dependent on ATP in multiple cell types, including cECs.
source: It is well established that lipid kinases involved in PIP2 synthesis require millimolar ATP for their activity (Balla and Balla, 2006; Hilgemann, 1997; Knight and Shokat, 2005; Suer et al., 2001), and it has been amply demonstrated that PIP2 maintenance is dependent on ATP in multiple cell types (Suh and Hille, 2008; Ye et al., 2018; Zakharian et al., 2011), including cECs (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIP2 has been reported to directly interact with different residues on the TRPV4 N-terminus in heterologous expression systems.
source: Notably, PIP2 has been reported to directly interact with different residues on the TRPV4 N-terminus in heterologous expression systems (Garcia-Elias et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Direct binding of PIP2 to the ankyrin repeat domain of the TRPV4 channel inhibits different modes of TRPV4 activation.
source: However, these studies reached discrepant conclusions, with one suggesting that direct binding of PIP2 to the ankyrin repeat domain of the TRPV4 channel inhibits different modes of TRPV4 activation (Takahashi et al., 2014) and the other reporting that PIP2 is necessary for heat-, hypotonicity- or epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (EET)-induced channel activation by facilitating structural rearrangements of the channel (Garcia-Elias et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PIP2 is necessary for heat-, hypotonicity- or epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (EET)-induced TRPV4 channel activation by facilitating structural rearrangements of the channel.
source: However, these studies reached discrepant conclusions, with one suggesting that direct binding of PIP2 to the ankyrin repeat domain of the TRPV4 channel inhibits different modes of TRPV4 activation (Takahashi et al., 2014) and the other reporting that PIP2 is necessary for heat-, hypotonicity- or epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (EET)-induced channel activation by facilitating structural rearrangements of the channel (Garcia-Elias et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 11,12-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (11,12-EET, 1 µM) evoked currents in cECs even in the absence of dialyzed PIP2.
source: Intriguingly, the putative endogenous TRPV4 channel activator (Earley and Brayden, 2015; Watanabe et al., 2003) 11,12-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (11,12-EET, 1 µM) evoked currents in cECs even in the absence of dialyzed PIP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results are the first to report PIP2-mediated suppression of TRPV4 channels in the endothelium and more broadly in native cells.
source: In any case, our results are the first to report PIP2-mediated suppression of TRPV4 channels in the endothelium and more broadly in native cells and are congruent with the results of Takahashi et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim represents a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Lipid molecules are tightly bound to the selectivity filter of the TRPV4 channel pore.
source: Interestingly, a recent study provided structural evidence that lipid molecules are tightly bound to the selectivity filter of the TRPV4 channel pore, although the identity and function of these lipids were not characterized (Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PGE2 has previously been postulated to act as an NVC agent through actions on Gs-coupled EP2/EP4 receptors in arteriolar smooth muscle.
source: We show here that PGE2, which has previously been postulated to act as an NVC agent through actions on Gs-coupled EP2/EP4 receptors in arteriolar smooth muscle (Lacroix et al., 2015; Zonta et al., 2003), activates TRPV4 channels in cECs independent of the action of the PIP2 metabolites, DAG and IP3, by relieving PIP2-mediated suppression (Figure 4, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GqPCR agonists exert the opposite effect on capillary Kir2.1 channels, inhibiting their ability to mediate capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling.
source: In contrast, we recently showed that GqPCR agonists exert the opposite effect on capillary Kir2.1 channels, inhibiting their ability to mediate capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A single GqPCR signaling cascade is capable of altering the balance between electrical Kir2.1 signaling (inhibition) and TRPV4 signaling (facilitation).
source: This two-way modulation (Figure 7) is unique as it indicates that a single GqPCR signaling cascade is capable of altering the balance between electrical Kir2.1 signaling (inhibition) and TRPV4 signaling (facilitation).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing bidirectional effects.

claim: GqPCR signaling-induced PIP2 depletion would likely depolarize cECs through the simultaneous disinhibition of depolarizing TRPV4 channels and deactivation of hyperpolarizing Kir2.1 channels.
source: Given the absence of Ca2+-activated K+ channels in cECs, noted above, GqPCR signaling-induced PIP2 depletion would likely depolarize cECs through the simultaneous disinhibition of depolarizing TRPV4 channels (this study) and deactivation of hyperpolarizing Kir2.1 channels (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and previous findings.

claim: The outward current through Kir2.1 channels at physiological membrane potentials (about −40 mV) and external K+ (3 mM) is ~6 fA.
source: Based on our direct Kir2.1 current measurements (Harraz et al., 2018; Longden et al., 2017) and the known voltage- and K+-dependence of Kir2.1 channels (Longden and Nelson, 2015), we estimate that the outward current through these channels at physiological membrane potentials (about −40 mV) and external K+ (3 mM) is ~6 fA.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from previous experimental data and known channel properties.

claim: Elevation of external K+ to 10 mM would increase Kir2 current at −40 mV to ~260 fA.
source: Elevation of external K+ to 10 mM would increase Kir2 current at this voltage to ~260 fA.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from known channel properties.

claim: The basal, PIP2-suppressed TRPV4 current at −40 mV is about −80 fA.
source: Our estimate of basal, PIP2-suppressed TRPV4 current at −40 mV is about −80 fA.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from experimental data.

claim: GqPCR activation increases TRPV4 open probability ~6 fold, producing a current (400–500 fA) sufficient to effectively short circuit K+-induced hyperpolarization.
source: GqPCR activation increases open probability ~6 fold, producing a current (400–500 fA) sufficient to effectively short circuit K+-induced hyperpolarization and cripple this key Kir2.1-based NVC mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from experimental data and inference about functional consequences.

claim: Activation of capillary GqPCRs should trigger Ca2+ signals in cECs through IP3-mediated Ca2+ release from intracellular stores and disinhibition of TRPV4 channels.
source: Activation of capillary GqPCRs should also trigger Ca2+ signals in cECs, presumably through IP3-mediated Ca2+ release from intracellular stores as well as disinhibition of TRPV4 channels (as described here) and subsequent Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and known signaling pathways.

claim: Capillary Ca2+ signals should positively influence hemodynamics through the Ca2+-dependent activation of nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and subsequent release of the vasodilator, NO.
source: Such capillary Ca2+ signals should positively influence hemodynamics—and thus functional hyperemia—providing a plausible explanation for the role of GqPCR agonists in the NVC process, presumably through the Ca2+-dependent activation of nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and subsequent release of the vasodilator, NO (Förstermann et al., 1991; Marziano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to previous studies.

claim: Local Ca2+ signals represent sites of PIP2 depletion and thus membrane potential depolarization.
source: Capillary Ca2+ signaling might also serve an entirely different purpose in functional hyperemia: because local Ca2+ signals represent sites of PIP2 depletion (through GqPCR signaling), and thus membrane potential depolarization (through TRPV4 disinhibition and Kir2.1 deactivation), they are likely to interfere with the progression of electrical signals generated further down the vascular tree.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Local Ca2+ signals may represent 'stop signs' or 'speed bumps' that play a role in redirecting hyperpolarizing (vasodilatory) signals away from certain brain areas.
source: Accordingly, these signals may represent 'stop signs' or 'speed bumps' that play a role in redirecting hyperpolarizing (vasodilatory) signals away from certain brain areas, in addition to their role in resetting the capillary membrane potential, noted above.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the functional role of Ca2+ signals.

claim: The exceedingly low basal TRPV4 activity and diminished sensitivity to GSK101 in cECs compared with mesenteric artery ECs suggest differences in the PIP2 'set point' in these two vascular beds.
source: Given the role of PIP2 in negatively regulating TRPV4 channels, the exceedingly low basal TRPV4 activity and diminished sensitivity to GSK101 in cECs (Figure 1) compared with mesenteric artery ECs (Sonkusare et al., 2012) suggest differences in the PIP2 'set point' in these two vascular beds.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: PIP2 levels in brain cECs are sufficient to saturate Kir2.1 channels and tune TRPV4 channel currents to levels that prevent inappropriate depolarization of the membrane potential.
source: Our data suggest that PIP2 levels in brain cECs are sufficient to saturate Kir2.1 channels (Harraz et al., 2018) and tune TRPV4 channel currents to levels that prevent inappropriate depolarization of the membrane potential (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and previous findings.

claim: In the absence of PIP2 suppression of TRPV4 channel-mediated inward currents, it is unlikely that increased outward K+ currents through Kir2.1 channels in response to elevated K+ would be sufficient to cause membrane potential hyperpolarization.
source: In the absence of PIP2 suppression of TRPV4 channel-mediated inward currents, it is unlikely that increased outward K+ currents through Kir2.1 channels in response to elevated K+ would be sufficient to cause membrane potential hyperpolarization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: Gnaq transcript levels in the mouse brain endothelium are reduced compared with those in peripheral pulmonary ECs.
source: Along these lines, a recent single-cell transcriptomics analysis showed that Gαq (Gnaq) transcript levels in the mouse brain endothelium are reduced compared with those in peripheral pulmonary ECs (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Brain cECs have higher mitochondrial content compared with other ECs.
source: Alternatively, differences in the set point could be indicative of more robust PIP2 synthesis in brain capillaries, a speculation that is supported by the higher mitochondrial content—and hence ATP synthesis—in highly active brain cECs compared with other ECs (Oldendorf and Brown, 1975; Oldendorf et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIP2 and its modulation by GqPCR agonists are major regulators of brain capillary signaling.
source: In conclusion, this study provides compelling evidence that brain capillaries express TRPV4 channels and further shows that the activity of these channels is physiologically suppressed by basal levels of PIP2. This introduces PIP2 and its modulation by GqPCR agonists as major regulators of brain capillary signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: When maintained at sufficient levels, PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels and supports capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling.
source: When maintained at sufficient levels, PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels and supports capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling, but in response to GqPCR activation, PIP2 levels are reduced, enhancing TRPV4 signaling and inhibiting retrograde electrical signaling via Kir2.1 channels.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In response to GqPCR activation, PIP2 levels are reduced, enhancing TRPV4 signaling and inhibiting retrograde electrical signaling via Kir2.1 channels.
source: When maintained at sufficient levels, PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels and supports capillary-to-arteriole electrical signaling, but in response to GqPCR activation, PIP2 levels are reduced, enhancing TRPV4 signaling and inhibiting retrograde electrical signaling via Kir2.1 channels.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Capillary GqPCRs can be envisioned as molecular switches that dictate the signaling modality in the brain microvasculature.
source: Capillary GqPCRs can therefore be envisioned as molecular switches that dictate the signaling modality in the brain microvasculature.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing the bidirectional effects of GqPCR activation.
